chapters.title: One step, two outcomes, one price
chapters.dek: Build a portfolio that pays whatever the option pays. Its cost is the option's price, and nothing about likelihood entered the calculation.

figures.title: The one-step tree, and the portfolio that reproduces it
figures.caption: Drag the real-world probability and watch the two bars in the lower panel behave completely differently. The blue one — what you expect to be paid — sweeps across the whole range. The vermilion one — what it costs to guarantee that payoff — does not move at all. Everything else on this page is a consequence of that gap.

figures.title: Build the replicating portfolio yourself
figures.caption: At the defaults the call pays 10 up and 0 down; half a share and 45 of borrowing match it exactly and cost 5. A dealer at 4.20 is then selling 5.00 of payoff for 4.20, and buying from him while selling your portfolio clears 0.80 in both states. Move the shares one notch off and the "arbitrage" pays more in one state and less in the other: it has become a bet.

checks.q: Two traders disagree completely about whether the stock will rise. One thinks 90% likely, the other 10%. What should they conclude about the option's price?
checks.right: They must agree on it. The price is the cost of a replicating portfolio, and that cost is determined by the two possible stock prices, not by the odds of reaching them
checks.why: They must agree. They will disagree violently about whether the trade is good — the optimist expects to make money buying it — but not about what it costs, because the cost is set by a portfolio both of them can construct and observe. That separation between value and expectation is the foundation the whole subject stands on, and it is why an options market can function between people with opposite views.

terms.Incomplete market: One where not every payoff can be manufactured from the traded instruments. Prices become a range rather than a point, and the gap is where a dealer's risk appetite lives.

chapters.text: Strip the problem to its smallest interesting version. A stock at 100. One period. Two possible outcomes: up to 110 or down to 90. A call struck at 100, which pays 10 in the up state and nothing in the down state. What is it worth? The instinct is to ask how likely the up state is, multiply, and discount. Hold that thought — it is the wrong question, and chapter 02 explains why. Ask instead: can I build something out of stock and cash that pays exactly 10 and 0 in those two states? Buy Δ shares and borrow B. In the up state the position is worth 110Δ − B ; in the down state 90Δ − B . Set those equal to 10 and 0 and you have two equations in two unknowns. Subtracting gives 20Δ = 10 , so Δ = 0.5 , and back-substituting gives B = 45 . So half a share, funded by 45 of borrowing, pays exactly what the call pays in both states. It costs 0.5 × 100 − 45 = 5 . That is the price. Any other price and you can buy the cheap one, sell the dear one, and collect the difference with no exposure at all — the portfolios are identical in every state of the world, so their prices must be too. Now the part worth sitting with. Slide the real-world probability of an up move across the figure. At P(up) = 0.01 the option's expected payoff is 0.10 . At P(up) = 0.99 it is 9.90 — a hundredfold difference in what you expect to receive. The replication cost, printed beside it, stays at 5.000000 throughout. Not approximately: the number never moves, because the probability never appeared in the derivation. This is the single most counterintuitive result in the subject, and the binomial model is where it is easiest to see, because you can watch it happen with two numbers and no calculus. [equation: Δ = (C_u − C_d) / (S_u − S_d) C = ΔS − B] Reads as: hold enough shares that their spread across the two outcomes matches the option's spread, then borrow whatever makes the low state come out right. The cost of that package is the option's value. The one-step tree, and the portfolio that reproduces it Expected payoff against replication cost, as the odds change The one period Drag the real-world probability and watch the two bars in the lower panel behave completely differently. The blue one — what you expect to be paid — sweeps across the whole range. The vermilion one — what it costs to guarantee that payoff — does not move at all. Everything else on this page is a consequence of that gap. Try this Set the probability of an up move to 99%. Predict the option's price before you look at the readout, then set it to 1% and predict again. Now solve it with your hands instead of algebra. Set the shares and the borrowing until your portfolio pays what the call pays in both states; the panel reads the tree above, so change the up and down moves there and you will have to solve again. Then a dealer offers you the call below what your portfolio costs. Buy the call, sell your portfolio, and see whether the profit is really free. Build the replicating portfolio yourself Your portfolio At the defaults the call pays 10 up and 0 down; half a share and 45 of borrowing match it exactly and cost 5. A dealer at 4.20 is then selling 5.00 of payoff for 4.20, and buying from him while selling your portfolio clears 0.80 in both states. Move the shares one notch off and the "arbitrage" pays more in one state and less in the other: it has become a bet. Trader's lens This is how a market maker thinks about every option on the screen: not "what is it worth" but "what does it cost me to make the same payoff out of things I can trade". The answer is their price, and a quote away from it is either an arbitrage or a sign their replication is missing something, usually a cost or a borrow. The hedge ratio comes first; the price is what the hedge costs. Nobody's view of the odds enters. Two traders who disagree about direction agree on the price. "Free money" is only free if the replication is exact. A near-miss is a position. Rule of thumb: before arguing about whether an option is cheap, write down the hedge that makes it cheap. Derivation — the two equations, and where the probability would have gone Write the replicating portfolio's value in each state and demand that it match the option. [equation: S_uΔ − B(1+r) = C_u S_dΔ − B(1+r) = C_d] Reads as: in the up state and in the down state, the shares minus the loan must equal the option. Two equations, two unknowns, no probabilities anywhere. Subtract the second from the first. The borrowing cancels because it is the same in both states — it is a certain amount, not a contingent one. [equation: Δ (S_u − S_d) = C_u − C_d] Reads as: the share count is fixed by matching the spread. This is delta, arrived at without differentiating anything. Substitute back for B and the price is C = ΔS − B . Notice what is absent: there is no place in either equation for a probability, because the equations describe every state rather than an average over states. That is the whole trick, and it is why the answer is a price rather than a forecast. Where it breaks. Two outcomes and two instruments is a square system, which is why it has a unique solution. Add a third possible outcome — a jump, a gap, a takeover at a different price — and you have three equations and two unknowns, no exact replication, and no single arbitrage-free price. The market is then said to be incomplete , and prices become a band whose width is somebody's risk appetite. Everything on this page assumes the world stays square.

chapters.title: The probability that is not a probability
chapters.dek: Rearrange the answer and a number between zero and one falls out. It is not a forecast, and treating it as one is the classic error.

figures.title: Two sets of weights on the same tree
figures.caption: The two distributions can be wildly different shapes and the option price only ever uses the vermilion one. Push the real-world drift up and the blue distribution marches right while the price readout sits still — the same result as chapter 01, now visible across a whole terminal distribution rather than two nodes.

checks.q: An option's price implies a 32% chance the stock finishes below 90. What can you conclude?
checks.right: That the insurance costs what a 32% chance would cost in a risk-neutral world. The real-world probability is lower, because the price includes compensation for bearing the risk
checks.why: It is a price, expressed in the units of a probability. Risk-neutral probabilities systematically overweight bad outcomes relative to reality, because people pay up for protection — which is exactly the risk premium the option price contains and the real-world probability does not. The third answer over-corrects: the number is highly informative, it just answers "what does this cost" rather than "what will happen".

terms.Risk-neutral probability: The weighting under which discounted expected payoffs give the right price. It is set by u, d and the interest rate — not a forecast, and systematically different from the real-world odds.

chapters.text: Take the price from chapter 01 and rearrange it. With a little algebra C = ΔS − B becomes something that looks startlingly like an expectation. Define p = (e^r·dt − d) / (u − d) . Then the price is exactly the discounted average of the two payoffs, weighted by p and 1−p. On our one-step example with zero rates, p works out to 0.500000 , and the discounted expectation is 5.000000 — the same answer replication gave, as it must be, because it is the same equation written differently. So there is a set of weights under which the naive "average the payoffs and discount" calculation is right. Those weights are the risk-neutral probabilities , and three things about them matter. They are not anybody's forecast. Nothing about the real world went into them — only u, d and the interest rate. If the true probability of an up move is 90%, p is still whatever the algebra says. They are exactly the weights that make the stock earn the risk-free rate. That is the defining property and the source of the name. Under p, the expected stock price is the forward. The figure checks it on a 200-step tree: the tree's expected terminal price is 105.12711 against a forward of 105.12711 , agreeing to the last digit shown. They exist because replication does. The reason you may price by taking an expectation under the wrong probabilities is that you were never really taking an expectation — you were pricing a portfolio, and the expectation is a bookkeeping device that produces the same number more conveniently. Get this backwards and you will believe the market is forecasting a 32% chance of a stock finishing below some level when it is doing nothing of the kind. What the market is telling you is what the insurance costs. Converting that into a real-world probability requires a risk premium that the option price does not contain. [equation: p = (e^r·dt − d) / (u − d) C = e^−r·dt [ p·C_u + (1−p)·C_d ]] Reads as: there is one weighting under which averaging the payoffs gives the right answer, and it is the one that makes the stock drift at the interest rate. Use it to compute; do not read it as a belief. chapters.title: Two outcomes become a thousand
chapters.dek: Chain the one-step argument and it becomes a lattice. Push the steps up and it becomes Black–Scholes.

figures.title: The lattice, with its terminal distribution
figures.caption: Notice how fast the shape of the terminal distribution settles and how slowly the price does. By ten steps the histogram already looks lognormal while the price is still wrong in the first decimal — the distribution converges much faster than the number does, which is why "it looks converged" is not a test.

checks.q: Your 200-step tree is accurate to about a cent. Roughly what does it cost to reach a tenth of a cent?
checks.right: Ten times the steps, and about a hundred times the work — the error falls like 1/N while the node count grows like N²
checks.why: Ten times the steps, a hundred times the work. First-order convergence combined with quadratic cost is why nobody brute-forces a tree to high precision — you either use the closed form where one exists, or you use the averaging trick in the next chapter, which buys about two decimal places for one extra tree.

terms.Recombining tree: Up-then-down lands on the same node as down-then-up, so N steps give N+1 endpoints instead of 2 to the N. It is what makes a lattice computable at all.

chapters.text: One step is a caricature — a stock with exactly two possible futures. The fix is not to abandon the argument but to repeat it. Split the year into N periods, let the stock move up or down in each, and apply chapter 01's replication at every node, working backwards from expiry. Two features make this practical. First the tree recombines : choosing d = 1/u means up-then-down lands exactly where down-then-up does, so N steps produce N+1 terminal prices rather than 2^N. A 500-step tree has 501 endpoints, not a number with 150 digits in it. Second, the up and down sizes are chosen so the tree's variance matches the volatility you are pricing with: u = e^σ√dt . That is the Cox–Ross–Rubinstein choice, and it is what makes the lattice converge to the same distribution Black–Scholes assumes. And converge it does. On a one-year at-the-money call at 30 volatility with rates at 5%, Black–Scholes says 14.2312 . A one-step tree says 16.9640 — off by more than two and a half. Ten steps gives 13.9408 . A hundred gives 14.2018 . Sixteen hundred gives 14.2294 , wrong in the third decimal. The rate of convergence is worth committing to memory because it is the honest answer to "how many steps do I need". Doubling N halves the error — measured across N = 50 to 1600 the ratio is 1.998, 1.999, 2.001, 2.002, 2.005 . That is first order : to get one more decimal place you need ten times the steps — and since the work grows with N², about a hundred times the work. Trees are not cheap. The figure draws the lattice with its node values and the convergence beside it. Watch the terminal distribution take shape as you add steps — by about thirty it is visibly a lognormal, which is the sense in which Black–Scholes is the limit of this construction rather than a separate theory. [equation: u = e^σ√dt d = 1/u dt = T/N] Reads as: make each step's up-move the size volatility says a step of that length should be, and make the down-move its exact reciprocal so the tree folds back on itself. The lattice, with its terminal distribution Convergence to Black–Scholes The tree Notice how fast the shape of the terminal distribution settles and how slowly the price does. By ten steps the histogram already looks lognormal while the price is still wrong in the first decimal — the distribution converges much faster than the number does, which is why "it looks converged" is not a test. Try this Step through N = 1, 2, 3, 4. Predict whether the price is approaching Black–Scholes from above, from below, or neither.

chapters.title: Convergence is a sawtooth, not a slope
chapters.dek: Adding one step can make a tree less accurate. Knowing why turns a nuisance into a free decimal place.

figures.title: Pricing error against step count
figures.caption: The vermilion trace is the sawtooth and the moss trace is the same information averaged in pairs. The averaged line is not merely smoother — it sits an order of magnitude closer to zero across the whole range, which is what makes this a fix rather than a cosmetic improvement.

checks.q: You price an option on a 100-step tree and again on 101 steps. The answers differ by six cents. What is wrong?
checks.right: Nothing. Consecutive trees straddle the true price because the strike sits differently against the terminal nodes depending on the parity of N. Average the two and you land within a fraction of a cent
checks.why: Nothing is wrong — that is the sawtooth. This is worth recognizing on sight, because the natural response is to hunt for a bug that does not exist. The disagreement between the two trees is itself the useful signal: it is roughly twice the error in either one, so it tells you how far off you are, and averaging removes most of it.

chapters.text: The convergence table in chapter 03 hides something. The errors do not shrink smoothly toward zero — they alternate in sign, step by step, while their envelope decays. Look at four consecutive trees on the same option: N = 40 is low by 0.0734 , N = 41 is high by 0.0672 , N = 42 is low by 0.0699 , N = 43 is high by 0.0640 . So going from a 40-step tree to a 41-step tree does not improve the answer. It moves it to the other side of the truth by about the same distance. Anyone who has tried to tune a tree by nudging N has met this and usually concluded something was broken. The cause is where the strike sits relative to the terminal nodes. In a recombining CRR tree the terminal prices are S·u^2j−N , so when N is even one node lands exactly at the starting price and when N is odd the strike falls between two nodes. An at-the-money option therefore sees a structurally different terminal grid depending on the parity of N, and the pricing error inherits that alternation. Which points straight at the fix. If consecutive trees sit on opposite sides of the answer by roughly equal amounts, average them . Price with N and with N+1 and take the mean. On this option a 25-step tree is off by +0.1103 and the 25/26 average is off by −0.0012 — about ninety times better for one extra tree. At N = 400 the raw error is −0.0074 and the average is −0.0002 . This is the practical content of the chapter: an unaveraged tree is being needlessly bad, and the correction is one line of code. It also generalizes — the same idea underlies the Richardson extrapolation used to accelerate almost every first-order numerical scheme. The averaged line is not merely smoother — it sits an order of magnitude closer to zero across the whole range, which is what makes this a fix rather than a cosmetic improvement. Try this Move the strike away from the money and predict what happens to the sawtooth's amplitude. The mechanism in the prose tells you the answer.

chapters.title: What the lattice can do that the formula cannot
chapters.dek: Black–Scholes is faster, exact and closed-form. It also cannot price an American put, which is most of the equity option market.

figures.title: The same lattice, priced both ways
figures.caption: The shaded nodes are where the model would exercise, and their upper edge is the exercise boundary drawn as the staircase it really is. Take rates to zero and the shading vanishes entirely for the put — the same result page 04 proves analytically, arrived at here by a machine that was never told about it.

checks.q: Why can't Black–Scholes price an American put?
checks.right: Because it produces a value today and at expiry with nothing in between, and the American question is a decision at every intermediate price and time. The tree prices one because it values every node
checks.why: There is nothing in between. The closed form is a single expression for today's value; the American problem is a free-boundary problem whose answer is a decision rule across the whole price-time plane. The last answer is a common trap: parity is a European relation and does not hold as an equality for American options, which is precisely why page 04's put chapter needs a tree.

chapters.text: If the binomial model merely converged to Black–Scholes it would be a teaching device and nothing more. It survives on real desks because backward induction can answer questions the closed form cannot even express. The reason is structural. Black–Scholes gives you a value at expiry and a formula for today, with nothing in between. A tree gives you a value at every node — every combination of price and time the model considers possible — and once you have that, you can apply a rule at each one. Early exercise. At every node, compare the continuation value with what exercising would pay and take the larger. That single line converts a European pricer into an American one. On a one-year 100-strike put with spot at 80, 30 volatility and rates at 10%, the European value is 16.2413 and the American is 20.2680 — a premium of 4.0267 , or 24.8% of the option's value. Page 04 is about when that premium exists; this is the machinery that computes it. Discrete dividends. A real stock pays lumps on known dates, not a continuous yield. In a tree you subtract the dividend from the stock price at the nodes where it goes ex. There is no clean way to say that in a closed form. Barriers and path rules. Anything that depends on where the price has been — knock-outs, triggers, exercise windows — can be enforced node by node. The figure prices both styles on the same lattice and shades the nodes where exercising wins. Raise rates and the shaded region climbs; that region is the exercise boundary page 04 studies, drawn here as the discrete object the model actually computes rather than as a smooth curve. The honest cost: the tree is slower, it converges as a sawtooth, and every extra feature slows it further. Desks use closed forms where they exist and lattices where they do not, which in equities means lattices for most of the book. [equation: V_node = max( e^−r·dt[ pV_u + (1−p)V_d ] , exercise value )] Reads as: at every node, take the better of holding on and cashing in. Deleting the max turns it back into a European pricer, which is the whole difference between the two models. The same lattice, priced both ways The early-exercise premium against rates The contract The shaded nodes are where the model would exercise, and their upper edge is the exercise boundary drawn as the staircase it really is. Take rates to zero and the shading vanishes entirely for the put — the same result page 04 proves analytically, arrived at here by a machine that was never told about it. Try this Set rates to zero with the put selected. Predict whether any node stays shaded.

chapters.title: Greeks fall out of the lattice for free
chapters.dek: You already computed the neighboring nodes. Delta and gamma are differences between numbers you have.

figures.title: Tree greeks against the closed form, as steps increase
figures.caption: Switch between delta and gamma and watch how much noisier the second one is at the same step count. Gamma is a difference of differences, so it inherits the sawtooth twice — which is the practical reason tree gammas are usually computed on a finer lattice than the price needs.

checks.q: Which greek costs an extra tree to compute?
checks.right: Vega. Volatility is not a coordinate of the lattice — it is baked into u and d — so you must rebuild the tree with a bumped input and difference the two prices
checks.why: Vega, and rho for the same reason. Delta, gamma and theta are differences between nodes the tree already contains, because price and time are its two coordinates. Anything that changes the geometry of the lattice itself has to be priced by building a second lattice.

chapters.text: A tree gives you the option's value at nodes that surround today's price, which means it has already done the work for the first two derivatives. No re-pricing and no bumping required. Delta is the difference between the two nodes one step out, divided by the difference in stock price between them — which is exactly chapter 01's Δ, now read off a big tree instead of a small one. On the one-year at-the-money call, a 500-step lattice gives 0.624192 against Black–Scholes' 0.624252 : a gap of 6 × 10^−5 , well inside the price error at that step count. Gamma comes from three nodes two steps out, as a second difference. Theta comes almost free as well: the central node two steps out sits at the same stock price as today but two periods later, so the difference between them is the passage of time with nothing else changed. Vega and rho are the exceptions. Neither volatility nor the interest rate is a coordinate of the lattice — they are baked into u, d and p — so getting those requires rebuilding the tree with a bumped input and differencing. That asymmetry is worth knowing when you are counting how expensive a full greek set is: delta, gamma and theta are nearly free, and every other greek costs another tree. One caution the figure makes visible. Because the price itself oscillates with N, so do the greeks read off it — and gamma, being a second difference, is noisier than delta. If a tree-derived gamma looks unstable across step counts, the tree is not broken; you are differencing a sawtooth. [equation: Δ ≈ (V_u − V_d) / (S_u − S_d) Θ ≈ (V_ud − V_0) / 2dt] Reads as: delta is the slope between the two nodes beside you and theta is the change at the node directly ahead of you. Both are differences between values the tree has already computed. Tree greeks against the closed form, as steps increase What to read Switch between delta and gamma and watch how much noisier the second one is at the same step count. Gamma is a difference of differences, so it inherits the sawtooth twice — which is the practical reason tree gammas are usually computed on a finer lattice than the price needs.

chapters.title: Where it breaks
chapters.dek: A tree with too few steps is not merely inaccurate. It can be arbitrageable.

figures.title: The risk-neutral weight, and the band it has to stay inside
figures.caption: Drag volatility down or rates up and watch p climb out of the band. The readout names the step count at which the tree becomes admissible again — which is a number worth computing before trusting any lattice on a low-volatility, high-rate underlying.

checks.q: Your tree returns p = 1.08. What does that mean?
checks.right: The model is arbitrageable: cash grows faster than even the up move, so the price it returns is not a price. Shorten the steps until p is back inside (0, 1)
checks.why: The tree contains an arbitrage. p above one means e^r·dt > u : cash grows faster than the stock's best case, so shorting the stock and lending is riskless profit. The dangerous part is that nothing throws an error — you get a plausible number back. The fourth answer inverts the fix: it is low volatility, not high, that causes this.

chapters.text: The risk-neutral weight p = (e^r·dt − d)/(u − d) is only a probability when it lands between zero and one. Nothing in the construction guarantees that, and when it fails the tree stops describing any coherent market at all. The condition is that the risk-free growth over one step must sit between the down move and the up move: d < e^r·dt < u . With the CRR choice that reduces to a neat requirement on the step length. Fail it on one side and the model says cash beats the stock even in the stock’s best case; fail it on the other and the stock beats cash even in its worst. Either is a free lunch, and every example below is the first kind — p above one. Concretely: at 10% volatility with rates at 8% , a two-year option priced on a single step gives p = 1.0761 . Stretch it to four years and p is 1.3867 . At 5% volatility with 10% rates, even a one-year single step gives 1.5388 . Low volatility and high rates is exactly the combination that breaks it, and it is not an exotic corner — it is short-dated rates products and low-volatility credit-like underlyings. The fix is more steps, since the requirement is a bound on dt : keeping each step shorter than (σ/r)² years is sufficient. It is worth checking rather than assuming, because a tree with p outside the unit interval does not crash. It returns a number, and the number is wrong in a way that no amount of eyeballing will reveal. Three further limits worth naming. Convergence is first order and the cost is quadratic. Chapter 03's arithmetic — ten times the steps for one more decimal, at a hundred times the work — is the reason lattices lose to closed forms and to finite-difference schemes wherever those are available. The tree's distribution is not the world's. Everything here inherits Black–Scholes' assumption of constant volatility and continuous, jump-free movement. A recombining lattice with fixed u and d cannot represent a volatility smile at all, which is why the model is a pricing engine rather than a description of the market — page 07 is the correction. Discrete dividends break recombination. Subtracting a fixed cash amount at an ex-date means up-then-down no longer lands where down-then-up does, and the tree stops folding. The usual repair is to build the lattice on the dividend-stripped price and add the dividend's present value back, which restores recombination at the cost of an approximation that page 04 flags in its own derivation. [equation: d < e^r·dt < u ⟺ dt < (σ / r)²] Reads as: each step must be short enough that volatility can outrun the interest rate over it. Violate it and the tree contains an arbitrage rather than a price. The risk-neutral weight, and the band it has to stay inside The parameters Drag volatility down or rates up and watch p climb out of the band. The readout names the step count at which the tree becomes admissible again — which is a number worth computing before trusting any lattice on a low-volatility, high-rate underlying. chapters.title: Drill it, then check yourself
chapters.dek: One-step trees are the arithmetic worth having automatic, because every larger tree is this repeated.

figures.caption: Core asks for hedge ratios and risk-neutral weights; Full adds replication costs and the step-size limit. The working is shown every time, right or wrong.

checks.q: A stock at 100 goes to 110 or 90. A 100-strike call is worth 5. What happens to that price if the up move becomes twice as likely?
checks.right: Nothing. The price is the cost of half a share funded by 45 of borrowing, and neither number depends on the odds
checks.why: Nothing at all. The replicating portfolio pays the option's payoff in both states, so its cost is fixed by the two stock prices rather than by their likelihoods. What changes is whether the trade is attractive, not what it costs.

checks.right: The weighting under which the stock's expected growth equals the risk-free rate. It is set by u, d and r, and contains no view about the real world
checks.why: The weighting that makes the stock drift at the risk-free rate. On a 200-step tree the implied expected terminal price is 105.12711 against a forward of 105.12711 — that identity is the definition, not a coincidence.

checks.q: Doubling the number of steps in a CRR tree does what to the pricing error?
checks.right: Halves it. Measured ratios across N = 50 to 1600 run 1.998 to 2.005, which is first-order convergence
checks.why: Halves it. First-order convergence with quadratic cost is the tree's central weakness, and it is why the averaging trick in chapter 04 matters so much in practice.

checks.q: Why do consecutive step counts give prices on opposite sides of the true value?
checks.right: Because the terminal nodes sit at S·u^(2j−N), so the strike lands on a node when N is even and between nodes when N is odd. The grid geometry alternates with parity
checks.why: The strike's position against the terminal grid alternates with parity. Recognizing this on sight saves a bug hunt, and averaging N with N+1 turns the nuisance into roughly two extra decimal places.

checks.q: What single change turns a European tree pricer into an American one?
checks.right: Taking the maximum of the continuation value and the exercise value at every node
checks.why: One max at every node. That the American problem reduces to a single line is the reason lattices remain standard equipment — on a one-year 100-strike put with spot at 80 and rates at 10%, that line is worth 4.03 on a 16.24 option.

checks.q: Which combination is most likely to push p outside (0, 1)?
checks.right: Low volatility and high rates, with few steps. The requirement is dt < (σ/r)², so a long step on a quiet underlying with expensive money fails it
checks.why: Low volatility, high rates, long steps. At 5% volatility and 10% rates a one-year single step gives p = 1.5388 — and the tree returns a number rather than an error, which is what makes the condition worth checking rather than assuming.
